content: This is an updated review of medical interventions for high-grade vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), a pre-cancerous condition of the vulval skin. High-grade VIN, also referred to as usual-type VIN (uVIN), VIN 2/3, or high-grade vulval intraepithelial lesion, is strongly associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and has the potential to progress to vulval cancer. Due to this risk, active management is typically recommended. However, there is no consensus on the optimal treatment approach, and surgical interventions are often associated with high morbidity and relapse rates, making non-surgical options more desirable. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of non-surgical (medical) treatments for high-grade VIN. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed non-surgical interventions in women diagnosed with high-grade VIN. A systematic search of databases and clinical trial registers was conducted, and five trials involving 297 women met the inclusion criteria. These trials evaluated topical imiquimod, topical cidofovir, and indole-3-carbinol at different doses. Three trials compared topical imiquimod 5% cream to placebo. Meta-analysis of these trials demonstrated that women treated with imiquimod were significantly more likely to achieve an overall response (complete or partial) at five to six months compared to those receiving placebo. Specifically, 58% of women in the imiquimod group showed a complete response, while none in the placebo group did. The evidence supporting this finding was of high quality. One trial provided 12-month follow-up data, showing that the treatment effect was sustained, with 38% of women in the imiquimod group achieving a complete response compared to none in the placebo group. Progression to vulval cancer was rare, with one case in the imiquimod group and two in the placebo group. Adverse events, such as erythema, erosion, pain, and pruritus at the lesion site, were more common in the imiquimod group, and dose reductions were more frequently required in this group. Quality of life (QoL) outcomes were reported in one trial, with no significant differences between the imiquimod and placebo groups. One trial compared topical imiquimod to topical cidofovir. At six months, the overall response rates were similar between the two groups, with 57% of women in the imiquimod group and 62% in the cidofovir group responding to treatment. Complete response rates were also comparable, at 45% and 46%, respectively. Adverse events were slightly more common in the imiquimod group, and there were slightly more treatment discontinuations in this group. Longer-term response data from this trial are awaited. A small trial comparing lowand high-dose indole-3-carbinol provided limited data and did not contribute significantly to the overall findings. The authors concluded that topical imiquimod appears to be a safe and effective treatment for high-grade VIN, although local side effects may require dose adjustments. Longer-term follow-up data are needed to confirm the durability of treatment responses and to assess the impact on progression to vulval cancer. Topical cidofovir may be a viable alternative to imiquimod, but further evidence is required, particularly regarding long-term outcomes. Additionally, five ongoing randomized trials are expected to provide further insights into various interventions for high-grade VIN.
